opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the best way to understand spatial intelligence is to go back to evolution. Long before there was language, before humans even existed, animals were perceiving and acting in a three-dimensional world. When the first trilobites developed eyes about 540 million years ago, that set off an evolutionary arms race. Seeing wasn't just passive; it was tied to moving, to hunting, to escaping, to surviving. So over hundreds of millions of years, nature built intelligence around understanding space: where things are, how they relate to each other, how they move, and how I can interact with them.

Language is incredibly powerful. It's what makes us human in many ways, and large language models have shown us how much can be captured in text. But language is a relatively recent invention, maybe a few hundred thousand years old. It's also a lossy, one-dimensional encoding of a world that is fundamentally 3D, physical, and governed by physics. If you only have words, you're missing a huge part of what intelligence actually is.

So when I talk about spatial intelligence, I mean the ability of a machine to perceive, reason about, generate, and interact with the 3D world, and the 4D world when you add time. It's not just recognizing a cup in an image, which is what a lot of computer vision did for years, including ImageNet. It's understanding that the cup has a shape and a back side you can't see, that it sits on a table, that if you push it, it might fall, and that you could pick it up by the handle. That's a much deeper representation of the world.

I believe this is a fundamental capability, not a niche application, because so much of what we want AI to do depends on it. Robotics obviously needs it, but so do design, architecture, manufacturing, gaming, the creative industries, augmented and virtual reality, and even scientific discovery. Think of how Watson and Crick reasoned about the 3D structure of DNA. Humans use spatial reasoning constantly to create and to understand.

That's why I say if we want truly general AI, AI that can be a real partner to humans in the world we actually live in, we can't stop at language. We need models that understand the world as a world. That's the problem I'm most excited about, and why I think it's the next frontier.

r001.rationale: The response says spatial intelligence includes reasoning about the 3D world.

r002.rationale: It explicitly includes generating the 3D world as part of spatial intelligence.

r003.rationale: It describes evolution as building intelligence around understanding space over hundreds of millions of years.

r004.rationale: It says truly general AI cannot stop at language and needs models that understand the world, clearly presenting spatial intelligence as necessary for complete AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think of spatial intelligence as the ability to perceive, understand, reason about, and act within the three-dimensional world. And I actually believe it's older and more fundamental than language. If you look at evolution, animals had vision and spatial understanding for hundreds of millions of years before anything like language emerged. A trilobite in the ocean 540 million years ago could sense light, and from that moment, perception and movement started co-evolving. The nervous system got bigger because animals needed to navigate, find food, avoid predators, and manipulate their environment. That is spatial intelligence. Language came much, much later, and really only in humans.

So when I look at today's large language models, I'm genuinely impressed, but I also see that language is a lossy, one-dimensional serialization of a world that is fundamentally three-dimensional, dynamic, and physical. You cannot fully describe in words how to catch a ball, or how the light falls on an object as you walk around it, or how a surgeon's hand moves in a cavity. Those things live in space and time, not in tokens of text.

For AI, that means we need models that can take in the world through perception, whether that's images, video, depth, or sensor data, and build an internal representation that respects geometry, physics, and the relationships between objects. Then they need to be able to reason over that representation, imagine what happens next, and generate actions or even new worlds. That's why I've been talking about world models rather than just vision models. Recognizing a cat in a photo was the ImageNet era. Understanding that the cat is on the table, that the table is near the edge of the room, that if I push the cup it will fall, and being able to generate or simulate that whole scene, is the next frontier.

And I think this matters practically, not just intellectually. Robotics, augmented reality, design, manufacturing, healthcare, scientific discovery. All of these are embodied in physical space. If we want AI to actually help people in the real world, and not just in chat windows, spatial intelligence is the missing piece. It's the capability that connects seeing to doing.

r001.rationale: It describes reasoning about a representation of the three-dimensional world, including geometry, physics, and object relationships.

r002.rationale: It includes the ability to generate actions or new worlds and to generate or simulate a scene.

r003.rationale: It says spatial understanding predates language in animal evolution and that perception and movement co-evolved.

r004.rationale: It calls spatial intelligence the missing piece for AI to help people in the real world.

astra-6.text:
I think of spatial intelligence as the ability to understand and interact with the three-dimensional world. It’s not just recognizing what’s in an image. It’s understanding how things relate to one another, what might happen next, and how your own actions can change the scene.

Imagine picking up a cup. You need to understand where it is, its shape, how to reach it, and how to grasp it without knocking something else over. We do this so naturally that we forget how much intelligence it requires. It connects perception, prediction, and action.

Language gives us a powerful way to describe the world, but a description doesn’t capture everything we need to operate in it. Spatial intelligence is fundamental because it allows an intelligent system to move beyond describing things toward understanding and acting in the world. And that matters both for robots in physical environments and for systems that help us create and explore virtual ones.

r002.rationale: It mentions systems that help create virtual environments, but does not identify generating three-dimensional worlds as a component of spatial intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss life’s evolutionary journey or its connection to spatial intelligence.

r004.rationale: It calls spatial intelligence fundamental, but does not assert that AI would be incomplete without it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think spatial intelligence is the ability to understand and interact with the three-dimensional world. When we look around a room, we don’t just recognize objects. We understand where they are, how they relate to each other, what we can reach, and what might happen if we move something. Much of that happens without our putting it into words.

For AI, that means going beyond identifying what’s in an image. A system needs to reason about geometry, depth, motion, and physical relationships. If a robot is going to pick up a cup, recognizing “cup” is only the beginning. It has to understand the cup’s shape, where to grasp it, and how its own movement will affect it.

What makes this fundamental is the connection between perception and action. Intelligence isn’t only about describing the world; it’s also about being able to act in it, anticipate consequences, and learn from those interactions. Language is an extraordinary part of intelligence, but the physical world has a structure that language alone doesn’t fully capture. Spatial intelligence is a way of grounding AI in that structure.

r002.rationale: It discusses understanding and acting in the physical world, but does not identify generating three-dimensional worlds as part of spatial intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not mention life’s evolutionary journey or connect it to the evolution of spatial intelligence.

r004.rationale: It calls spatial intelligence fundamental and says AI needs spatial reasoning, but does not clearly assert that AI would be incomplete without it.
